newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-British Energy sees output flat.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-British Energy sees output flat.

text.p: Nuclear power generator British Energy Plc, posting its first results since flotation, said on Thursday it expected its electricity output for the year to be roughly the same as last year. The company said it did not expect the trend of higher prices in the market seen in the first half to continue for the rest of the year.

"The prices in the summer period have been somewhat higher, but we don't expect that to continue through the winter, half- on-half. And we expect the year-end output to be roughly the same as last year," chief executive Robert Hawley told Reuters.
He added in an interview that he hoped the firm's full-year output would be "a little bit better" than the 61.2 Terawatt hours it had last year.

British Energy's output rose 12 percent to 31.5 Terawatt hours in the first half, boosted by problems at its competitors' plants. A Terawatt hour, the largest unit of measurement for electricity sales, represents one billion kilowatt hours.

British Energy, which was floated on the London Stock Exchange in July, reported a pro forma loss after taxation of 32 million stg for the first half to September 30 compared to a loss of 169 million stg in the year-earlier period.
The firm also said it agreed to supply electricity to Southern Electric Plc for up to 15 years, expanding the companies' existing relationship.
Hawley declined to give financial details, but he did say the deal would increase British Energy's sales to Southern.
Last year, the company sold Southern Electric 6.5 Terawatt hours, representing about 15 percent of British Energy's output in England and Wales.
"What we're looking at now is a situation where it will be somewhat north of that for a period of 15 years," Hawley said.

"And of course from our point of view, the advantage is it gives us a degree of longer-term price stability which hedges against the uncertainty in pool prices," he added. Hawley said the company was talking to other regional electricity companies (RECs), as well as other firms, about similar deals.
"This is not an exclusive deal, because we've still got other electricity to sell," he said.
He added the company was focusing on increasing output and cost-savings at its existing assets but would also consider joint ventures in the UK and investments overseas.
When asked whether the firm had any such investments in the pipeline, Hawley said, "We do, but I can't tell you."
British Energy set an interim dividend of 4.6p per share, in line with its previous estimates.
"If the wind's in the right direction, and all sorts of things, we are pretty confident we'll meet our final dividend of 13.7p," Hawley said.
British Energy's shares slid 1/2p to 135 by 0935 GMT.
